en.s4.li1: Meta (Instagram and Facebook). Meta requires people to use its AI disclosure tool when they post organic content with photorealistic video or realistic-sounding audio that was digitally created or altered, and it may apply penalties to people who don't. Meta also adds an "AI info" label when it detects industry-standard signs that content was made with AI, or when the person posting discloses it. On ads, Meta labels images created or significantly edited with AI, with "AI info" in the "About this ad" screen, and ads about social issues, elections or politics have their own mandatory AI disclosure.
en.s4.li2: The FTC. Its Consumer Reviews and Testimonials Rule has no blanket ban on AI-generated avatars in marketing. But fake or false testimonials are prohibited, and the FTC warns that avatars can still be deceptive under the FTC Act. Its endorsement guidance sums it up: endorsements must be honest and not misleading.
en.s4.li3: New York. A New York law (S8420-A), now signed and in effect, requires commercial ads to conspicuously disclose when they include a "synthetic performer": an AI-generated person who isn't a recognizable real performer. Penalties are $1,000 for a first violation and $5,000 for each one after that. Audio-only ads are exempt. If your ads reach people in New York, keep it in mind.
en.s4.li4: Florida. Florida's AI disclaimer law (s. 106.145) is about political ads, not regular business ads.
en.s4.p1: Short answer: for realistic AI video on Instagram and Facebook, yes, use the label. Here's what the official sources say:
en.s4.p2: My own practice is simpler than any of these rules: I label every AI video. It says so on screen and in the caption. On Instagram and Facebook, the post should also carry Meta's AI label, since its rules ask for it on realistic AI video. Nobody should have to guess.
en.s4.p3: This is general information, not legal advice. For a specific situation, talk to a lawyer.

en.s5.p1: Honest answer: I haven't seen Meta publish anything saying a correct AI label lowers reach, and I'm not going to guess.
en.s5.p2: What Instagram has said points the other way. Its "AI-generated profile" label is for profiles that feature an AI-generated person, and Instagram warns that creators who don't label those profiles appropriately may see limits to their reach. That's about whole profiles, not single posts, but the risk Instagram has named is not labeling. Being upfront is the safer path, and it's the right one for your customers.

es.s4.li1: Meta (Instagram y Facebook). Meta exige usar su herramienta de divulgación de IA cuando publicas contenido orgánico con video fotorrealista o audio que suena real y que fue creado o alterado digitalmente, y puede aplicar sanciones a quien no lo haga. También pone la etiqueta "AI info" cuando detecta señales estándar de la industria de que el contenido se hizo con IA, o cuando quien publica lo declara. En los anuncios, Meta etiqueta las imágenes creadas o muy editadas con IA, con "AI info" en la sección "About this ad", y los anuncios sobre temas sociales, elecciones o política tienen su propia divulgación de IA obligatoria.
es.s4.li2: La FTC. Su regla sobre reseñas y testimonios no prohíbe de forma general los avatares generados con IA en el mercadeo. Pero los testimonios falsos sí están prohibidos, y la FTC advierte que un avatar igual puede ser engañoso bajo la Ley de la FTC. Su guía sobre recomendaciones lo resume: tienen que ser honestas y no engañosas.
es.s4.li3: Nueva York. Una ley de Nueva York (S8420-A), ya firmada y vigente, obliga a que los anuncios comerciales indiquen de forma visible cuando aparece un "intérprete sintético": una persona generada con IA que no es un artista real reconocible. Las multas son de $1,000 la primera vez y $5,000 por cada infracción después. Los anuncios solo de audio están exentos. Si tus anuncios llegan a gente en Nueva York, tenlo en cuenta.
es.s4.li4: Florida. La ley de Florida sobre avisos de IA (s. 106.145) es para anuncios políticos, no para la publicidad normal de un negocio.
